transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, it's... it's hard to explain exactly when it all started, but mostly I just don't feel like myself anymore. I mean, I've always been a guy who gets things done, you know? You have to be in my line of work. Being in protective services, you have to be on the ball, alert, always moving, always ready to respond. I worked hard for my bachelor's degree, worked hard to get where I am. But lately... I just feel completely hollowed out. 

I stopped doing everything that used to make me, well, me. I stopped hiking. I used to go up the trails at the state park every single weekend with my gear, just to get away and breathe the air, but I haven't been out there in months. I stopped coaching the youth league, which I used to love. I stopped playing my guitar—it's an old acoustic I've had for twenty years, and now it just sits in the corner gathering dust because I can't even bear to pick it up. I don't even call people back anymore. My friends, my coworkers, they leave voicemails and I just stare at the phone. It's not that I don't care, it's just... I don't know. 

I live in this small rental right now, and honestly, some days I just sit in there for hours. I'll sit on the edge of the couch, or just at the kitchen table, staring at nothing for hours on end. And the most frustrating part is that I know there are things to do. The whole time I'm sitting there, my brain is listing off all the chores—the laundry piling up, the mail I need to open, the fact that I need to shower or eat a real meal—so I know I need to get up. But I just can't make myself start. It's like the starter motor in my head is completely blown. I just sit there frozen, wasting the entire day, and I can't seem to break out of it no matter how hard I tell myself to just move.
Have you noticed that things you used to enjoy, like hiking or playing guitar, no longer interest you or make you feel good?

Yeah, exactly, exactly. It’s like… the joy is just gone. Completely drained out of everything. I mean, the hiking, for instance. I used to map out these elaborate routes, you know? I’d check the weather, pack my gear—the good boots, the hydration pack, the emergency kit, because in my line of work, you always have to be prepared. I’d get up at dawn, drive up to the state park, and just… breathe. It felt good. It made me feel alive. But now? The thought of even finding my boots feels like trying to climb a mountain before I’ve even left the house. I haven't been out there in months. 

And the guitar… man, I’ve had that acoustic for twenty years. Since college. I used to just sit on the porch and strum for hours, learning new songs, playing old ones. It was my way to decompress after a long shift. Now it’s just sitting there in the corner of my rental, gathering dust. I look at it, and I know I should pick it up, I know it used to make me happy, but I just feel… nothing. No spark. No interest. 

Same with coaching the youth league. I loved those kids. I loved teaching them the game, seeing them improve, but I just stopped showing up. I stopped calling people back. My phone will ring, and I’ll see my buddy’s name on the screen, or a coworker checking in, and I just stare at it until it goes to voicemail. And then I’ll just sit there. I’ll sit on the edge of the couch, or at the kitchen table, for hours. Just staring. And the whole time, my brain is screaming at me, right? It’s saying, 'Get up, do the laundry, open the mail, take a shower, eat something real instead of just grabbing a handful of crackers.' I know all these things are piling up. I know I need to do them. But I just… I can’t make myself start. I can’t move. It’s like the connection between my brain saying 'do this' and my body actually doing it is just severed. I just sit there, wasting the whole day, feeling completely hollowed out. I just don't feel like myself anymore at all.
Have you had periods like this before, where you felt persistently down and lost interest in things you used to enjoy, or is this the first time you've experienced something like this?

No... no, I really haven't. I mean, this is completely new to me, which is probably why it's so incredibly frustrating. I've been on this earth for 45 years, and I have never, ever felt anything like this before. 

I mean, sure, I've had bad days. Everyone has bad days, right? Especially in protective services. You work a double shift, you deal with a high-stress situation, you get yelled at by the public, and you come home completely wiped out. But even then... even when I was absolutely exhausted to my bones, I never lost my drive. I'd sleep for ten hours, wake up, and I'd be right back at it. I'd grab my gear, go for a run, or I'd call up the guys and we'd go grab a beer or watch a game. I always bounced back. 

Even back in college, when I was grinding out my bachelor's degree—working nights just to pay tuition, studying until 3 AM, living off black coffee and whatever cheap food I could find—I was stressed, yeah. I was burnt out sometimes. But I never lost my interest in life. I never just... stopped caring. I always had my eye on the prize, always wanted to be out in the world doing things. If there was a problem, I fixed it. If there was a task, I got it done. 

But this? This is entirely different. It's not just being tired or having a rough week or needing a vacation. It's like... like someone went into the breaker box in my head and just completely cut the main power line. I've never felt this paralyzed before. I've always been a doer, a guy who takes action. And now I just sit there looking at the mail on the counter, knowing I should open it, remembering that I used to be the kind of guy who would sort it the second I walked through the door, and I just do nothing. So, no, to answer your question, nothing like this has ever happened to me in my entire life. It's completely out of left field, and honestly, it's messing with my head because I don't even recognize the guy sitting in my living room anymore. I just don't know where the old me went, or why he left.
Have you ever experienced a time in your life before this when you felt down nearly every day, lost interest in things you usually enjoy, and had trouble functioning for at least two weeks or more?

Like I was just saying, no, never. Not for two weeks, not even close. I mean, two weeks is a really long time to just be... out of commission, you know? In my line of work, if you're off your game for two whole weeks, people notice. Your supervisor notices, the guys on your shift notice. You can't just hide for fourteen days when you're doing protective services. You have schedules, you have rotations, you have mandatory briefings that you absolutely have to be at. 

I remember back in, I don't know, maybe 2010 or 2011, I had this really bad flu. I mean, it knocked me flat on my back, sweating through the sheets, couldn't even keep a glass of water down kind of flu. I was out of work for maybe five days, and even then, by day three I was going completely stir crazy. I was trying to read incident reports from my bed, trying to call in to see how the shift was handling the downtown detail because there was a big event going on. I couldn't stand just lying there doing nothing. My body was sick, sure, but my brain was still going a hundred miles an hour. I still cared about what was happening. 

So the idea of feeling down and losing interest in everything for two whole weeks? Prior to whatever this is that's happening to me right now? No. Never. Even when my old dog, Buster, passed away—I had him for twelve years, a golden retriever mix, just the absolute best dog you could ever ask for—I was crushed. I was absolutely devastated. I took two days off, I grieved, but then I was right back at work. I still went for my morning runs. I still picked up my guitar a few days later to play something quiet. I never just... stopped functioning day after day after day for weeks on end. 

This whole thing, this endless stretching out of just total nothingness where weeks go by and I haven't done a single thing... it's completely uncharted territory for me. I mean, if you had told me a year ago that I'd be sitting in my kitchen doing absolutely nothing for weeks, letting the mail pile up to the ceiling, I would have laughed in your face. It's just not who I am. Or... well, who I was, I guess. So, no, never two weeks. Never anything like this.
Have you ever had a period of time where you felt unusually high, extremely energetic, or so irritable that it was hard to control, where your behavior was out of character for you?

Unusually high? Like... extremely energetic? No, no, definitely not. I mean, I'm a pretty even-keeled guy. Or, well, I always was. In protective services, you know, you really can't be bouncing off the walls or flying off the handle. You have to maintain a baseline. If you're too hyped up, you make mistakes, you misjudge a situation, and in my job, mistakes mean people get hurt. So I've always prided myself on being steady. 

And as for being irritable... I mean, sure, I get annoyed. Who doesn't? You get a rookie on your shift who doesn't know how to properly log an incident, or you're stuck in gridlock traffic on the interstate after a 14-hour day, yeah, you get a little grumpy. You might swear at the steering wheel. But out of control? Doing things out of character? Never. I've never been the type to just snap or lose my temper in a way that scared anybody or made them think I was acting strange. 

And the energy thing... man, I wish. I mean, honestly, I really wish I had even a tenth of that kind of energy right now just to get up and take the trash out to the curb. But no, I don't think I've ever had a period where I felt unusually high or anything. I never went on any wild phases, never suddenly decided to stay up for three days straight remodeling the kitchen or, I don't know, driving to Vegas on a whim. My ex used to actually complain about it, saying I was too predictable, too routine-oriented. I like my schedules. I like knowing exactly what's coming next. I've never been one to get these huge, uncontrollable surges of energy where I'm acting like a different person. I was just... steady. Always steady. Just putting one foot in front of the other, day in and day out. Until the bottom completely dropped out of everything and now I'm just... stuck. So, no, to answer your question, I've never experienced anything even remotely close to that.
Have you ever had a period of time, even before this current one, where you felt down or lost interest in things for two weeks or more?

Doc, I... I feel like we're going in circles a bit here, because like I was just saying a minute ago, no. Never. Not before this current situation. 

I know you have to be thorough, and I respect that, I really do. In my line of work, we have protocols too, you know? You have to ask the same question from three different angles just to make sure the person isn't changing their story or hiding something. But my story isn't changing because it's just the plain truth. Before this started, I was always moving. The longest I ever even stepped away from my normal routine was maybe a week and a half, years ago, when I took some accumulated leave to help my brother replace the roof on his garage. 

And let me tell you, hauling bundles of heavy shingles up an aluminum ladder in the July heat is the exact opposite of losing interest in things. We were up at dawn, working until the sun went down, measuring, cutting, nailing. Then we'd grill out in the evenings and talk about the next day's work. I was completely engaged. I was present. I didn't have the time or the inclination to be down. My mind was always occupied with the next task, the next shift, the next... anything, really. 

So, to answer you again, honestly and completely: no. Before this current thing hit me—where I'm just paralyzed and can barely get off the couch—there was never a time in my forty-five years where I lost two whole weeks of my life to feeling down or empty. It just never happened.
How long have you been feeling this way? Has it been more than two years?

Well, no, it hasn't been two years. It's... let me think. The timeline gets a little blurry because the days just sort of bleed into one another now, but I know exactly when it started. It was right around the time I moved into the new place. The smaller rental, you know? After the divorce was finalized. The house—the one we bought together, the one with the big yard for Buster and the garage where I had my workbench—she kept that, which made sense, I guess. But I had to downsize. I had to pack up fifteen years of my life into cardboard boxes and move into this little two-bedroom duplex on the other side of town. 

That was about a year and two months ago. I remember because it was right before Thanksgiving last year. I was supposed to have the guys from my shift over for a turkey fry, something we used to do every year, but I just... I couldn't unpack the boxes. I couldn't find the fryer, I couldn't bring myself to go to the grocery store, and honestly, I couldn't even stand the thought of having people in that cramped little space asking me how I was doing. So I canceled. And that was really the start of it. 

Things just started unraveling from there. First it was just leaving the boxes unpacked, telling myself I'd get to it on my next day off. But then the days off would come and go, and I'd just sit there staring at the cardboard. Then it was the mail. Then it was the dishes. And before I knew it, a year had gone by, and I'm still sitting in a place that doesn't feel like home, surrounded by boxes I haven't opened, feeling like I'm completely detached from everything. So yeah, about fourteen months. A year and two months. Not two years, but still... it feels like a lifetime.
Have you ever had a period of time before this current one—lasting at least two weeks—where you felt down most of the day, nearly every day?

Doc, I... I feel like we're just hitting the exact same nail with the exact same hammer here. Like I said before, no. I really haven't. And I know you're just doing your job, I get that. In protective services, we have to ask the same thing a few different ways sometimes too, just to make sure we're getting the full picture, making sure the witness isn't changing their story or, you know, getting confused about the timeline. But my timeline is solid on this. Before this whole thing started—before the move, before the boxes piled up, before I just stopped being able to function—I was fine. I was always fine.

I never had a two-week stretch where I was just down in the dumps all day. I mean, sure, I've had bad days. Who hasn't? You work a double shift, you deal with a difficult situation at work, you come home and the hot water heater is busted... yeah, you're going to be in a bad mood for a day or two. You might just want to sit in front of the TV and not talk to anybody. But that's just life, right? That's just a normal reaction to stress. It never stretched into weeks. It never turned into this... this heavy blanket that just smothers everything. 

I was always the guy who bounced back. I'd get a good night's sleep, maybe go for a run—I used to run three miles every other morning, rain or shine, never missed it—and I'd be good to go. I had a routine. I had my schedule. And that schedule didn't allow for two weeks of feeling down. I had responsibilities. I had a mortgage, I had a wife, I had a dog. I had a job that required me to be sharp and focused. I couldn't afford to just check out for weeks at a time. So, no, before this current... whatever this is... I never experienced anything like that. I was steady. Always steady. Until I wasn't.
Have you ever had more than one separate period in your life when you felt down or lost interest in things you usually enjoy?

Doc, I... I really don't know how else to say this. We're asking the exact same question again, just dressed up in different clothes. No. I haven't had more than one period. I haven't had *any* periods before this current one. Like I've been saying, over and over, this is the first time in my entire forty-five years on this earth that I've ever felt this way. 

I don't mean to sound frustrated, I really don't, but I feel like I'm on the witness stand being cross-examined by a defense attorney who's trying to trip me up on a technicality. 'Did you feel down for two weeks?' 'Did you feel down most of the day?' 'Did you have more than one period of feeling down?' It's all the same answer, Doc. No. Zero. None. 

Before I moved into that duplex fourteen months ago, my life was a straight, solid line. I went to work, I did my job, I came home, I took Buster for a walk, I mowed the lawn on Saturdays, I watched the game on Sundays. I enjoyed all of it. I enjoyed my life. I enjoyed the guys at work, I enjoyed tinkering with my tools in the garage. I never had a time where I just lost interest in everything and checked out. Not once. Not twice. Never. This whole... paralysis, this not being able to open boxes or wash a dish or care about anything... this is brand new. And it's been going on for fourteen months straight. There are no separate periods. It's just one long, continuous nightmare that started when I signed that lease and hasn't stopped since.

Have you had more than one separate time in your life when you felt down or lost interest in things you usually enjoy, each lasting at least two weeks, with at least two months in between those times where you felt better?

Doc, I... I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall here, or maybe you're just required to read every single variation of this off a clipboard, but we are going in circles. Honestly, it’s like when we have to interrogate a suspect and we just keep asking the same thing, hoping they slip up. But I’m not slipping up, because the truth is just the truth. 

No. Absolutely not. There hasn't been any two-month period where I felt better. There haven't been multiple separate times. 

Like I just told you, before fourteen months ago, before the divorce and the move to that cramped little duplex, there were zero periods of feeling down. None. I was steady as a rock. I did my job, I ran my three miles, I took care of my house. And then, fourteen months ago, the bottom fell out. And since the bottom fell out, I haven't climbed back up. Not for two months, not for two weeks, not for two days. 

If I had a two-month stretch in the middle of this past year where I actually felt like my old self, don't you think I would have unpacked my kitchen? Don't you think I would have finally taken the tape off those cardboard boxes and at least found my good coffee maker instead of drinking that burnt sludge from the gas station on the corner every single morning? But I haven't. The boxes are exactly where the movers dropped them over a year ago. 

There is no roller coaster here, Doc. There’s no dipping down for a couple of weeks, coming up for air for a couple of months, and going back down. It’s just one long, continuous drop that started right before Thanksgiving last year, and I've just been sitting at the bottom ever since. So, no. No separate times, and definitely no two months of feeling better in between. Just this. Just... whatever this past year has been.

Have you had more than one separate time in your life when you felt down or lost interest in things you usually enjoy, each lasting at least two weeks, with at least two months in between those times where you felt better?

Doc, I... look, I know you're just doing your job, reading off the form, but I feel like I'm losing my mind here, and not in the way you're probably writing down on that pad. We've literally just covered this. It's the exact same question, just... longer. 

No. The answer is still no. There are no separate times. There are no two-month breaks. There are no vacations from this. I haven't had a single day in the last fourteen months where I woke up and thought, 'Hey, maybe I'll open a box today. Maybe I'll find my running shoes. Maybe I'll actually care about something.' It just hasn't happened. 

I don't know how to make it any clearer. Before the divorce, before I moved into that duplex, I was fine. I was the guy who handled things. I was the guy who kept everyone else calm when things went sideways at work. I didn't get depressed. I didn't lose interest in things. I liked my life. And then... I just stopped. And it's been one continuous, unbroken line of just... nothing. No ups, no downs, just a flatline. 

If there had been a two-month break, believe me, I would have noticed. My dog would have noticed. I would have taken Buster to the park instead of just letting him out the back door while I stared at the wall. I would have done *something*. But I haven't. So, no. No separate times. No two-month breaks. Just this one, long, fourteen-month stretch of whatever the hell this is. I really, really don't know how else to explain it to you, Doc.

Have you ever had more than one separate time in your life when you felt down or lost interest in things you usually enjoy, each lasting at least two weeks, with at least two months in between those times where you felt better?

Doc, I'm... I'm really trying to keep my patience here, but I swear on my badge, if you ask me this exact same question one more time, I might just walk out of this room. I mean, are you listening to me? Are you actually hearing the words coming out of my mouth, or is this some kind of psychological test to see how long it takes for a guy to snap? Because it feels like a test. It really does. 

We just went over this. We just went over it, and we went over it before that, and before that. The answer hasn't magically changed in the last thirty seconds. No. Capital N, capital O. No. 

There has never been another time. Not when I was in my twenties, not when I was in my thirties, not when I first started on the force, not when I got married, not when I got promoted. Never. I was a guy who got up, put his boots on, and handled his business. I didn't sit around moping. I didn't lose interest in things. I liked fishing, I liked working on my truck, I liked my life. 

And then, fourteen months ago, everything just... stopped. The divorce happened, I moved into that duplex, and the switch just flipped off. And it hasn't flickered back on. Not for two months, not for two weeks, not for two minutes. It's been one long, endless, suffocating stretch of just... nothing. I haven't unpacked a single box. I haven't cooked a single meal. I haven't felt like myself for over a year. 

So please, Doc, I'm begging you, write it down in big bold letters on that clipboard of yours. No separate times. No breaks. Just this one, continuous, fourteen-month nightmare. Can we please, for the love of God, move on to a different question now?

Before the past year, have you ever had a time when you felt down or lost interest in things for at least two weeks, then felt better for at least two months, and then had another time like that again?

Doc, I... I just... I don't know what else to say. I really don't. Are you... is there a camera in here? Is this some kind of hidden camera show, or... or is this a tactic? Like when we bring a suspect into the box and we just ask them the exact same thing, over and over and over, just rephrasing it slightly, trying to see if they'll crack and change their story? Because I'm not a suspect, Doc. I'm just a guy sitting here trying to get some help, and you are literally asking me the exact same thing you just asked me three times in a row. 

I don't know how many different ways the English language allows me to say the word 'no'. 

Before the past year... before fourteen months ago, when my wife left and I had to pack my entire life into cardboard boxes and haul them over to that duplex... no. I never felt down like this. I never lost interest in things. Not for two weeks, not for two days. I was fine. I was the guy who was always fine. I was the guy who worked his shifts, did his overtime, came home, mowed the lawn, fixed the sink, and took the dog for a walk. I didn't have these... these episodes, or whatever you want to call them. 

And I definitely didn't have one, feel better for two months, and then have another one. I didn't have a first one to begin with! My life was just... normal. Stable. Predictable. Boring, maybe, but stable. 

I didn't know what it felt like to sit on a couch for three days straight without showering because the idea of standing under the water just felt like too much work. I didn't know what it felt like to look at my fishing gear—gear I used to spend hours cleaning and organizing—and feel absolutely nothing. Nothing at all. 

That all started fourteen months ago. And it hasn't stopped. It hasn't paused. It hasn't taken a two-month vacation. It just started, and it stayed. 

So, for the fourth time, or fifth time, or however many times we've done this little dance... no. Before this past year, I never had a time like that. Never. Not once. Can we please, please, just talk about something else? Anything else? Because I feel like I'm losing my mind having this same conversation over and over again.

Have you had more than one separate time in your life when you felt down or lost interest in things you usually enjoy, each lasting at least two weeks, with at least two months in between those times where you felt better?

Are you... are you actually kidding me right now? I honestly don't know if I should laugh or just get up and walk right out that door. Is your computer broken? Is the screen frozen on that one specific sentence? Because I feel like I'm trapped in the Twilight Zone here, Doc. 

Look, let me just... let me paint you a picture, okay? Let me walk you through my entire adult life so we can finally, definitively, put a nail in this specific question. From the day I graduated the academy, all the way up until I was forty-four years old, I was a rock. I woke up at 5:00 AM every single morning. I made my coffee—black, no sugar—I put on my uniform, I drove to the precinct, and I did my job. I didn't have 'separate times' of feeling down. I didn't have two weeks of losing interest in my life, let alone multiple times with little two-month vacations in between where everything was sunshine and rainbows. I went to ballgames. I went fishing. I took my ex-wife out to dinner at this little Italian place on 4th street every Friday. Every single Friday, like clockwork. I was fine. 

And then, fourteen months ago, the bottom just completely fell out. The divorce, the duplex, the boxes... and since that exact day, there hasn't been a single hour—not an hour, not a minute, and definitely not two whole months—where I felt like myself again. It is just one, giant, unbroken, heavy blanket over my entire existence. Buster just stares at me, wondering why we don't go to the park anymore, and I just sit there. Every day. For fourteen months straight. 

So... no. No, Doc. For the fifth time, or whatever number we're on now. I have never had separate times. I have never had a two-month break. I really, truly, do not have a different answer to give you. Can we please, please move on?

Before the past year, did you ever have a time when you felt down or lost interest in things for at least two weeks, then felt better for at least two months, and then had another time like that again?

Okay. Okay, I'm... I'm looking right at you, Doc, and I'm honestly trying to figure out if you're actually a real person right now, or if I'm just completely losing my grip on reality here. Because a real person hears what another person says. A real person doesn't just sit there and loop the exact same script like a... like a broken dispatch radio. You know when dispatch gets stuck? The signal just bounces off the repeater and you hear 'Unit 4, status... Unit 4, status...' over and over, and you're screaming into the mic 'I'm here, I'm here!' but they just keep saying it? That's what this feels like. It's like you're not even in the room with me. 

I have a bachelor's degree, okay? I've been on the force for over two decades. I am not a stupid man. I understand the words you are saying to me. 'Before the past year.' 'Two weeks.' 'Two months.' I hear you. I process the question. And I am giving you the answer. 

Listen to me carefully. Read my lips. Before the past year—before the fourteen months of absolute, crushing nothingness that I have been living in since the day the moving truck dropped my life off in cardboard boxes at that godforsaken duplex—no. The answer is no. 

I did not have two weeks of feeling down. I did not have a two-month recovery period. I didn't have a second time, or a third time, or a fourth time. My life was a straight line. A perfectly straight, unremarkable line. I worked, I came home, I ate dinner, I went to sleep. I didn't sit around analyzing whether I lost interest in my hobbies because my hobby was just... living. It was doing the job. I liked my truck. I liked my dog, Buster. I liked my wife. 

And then it all stopped. One time. Just once. Fourteen months ago. And it's still happening right now. I'm still in the exact same hole I fell into fourteen months ago. I haven't climbed out for two months to get some fresh air. I haven't had a break. I've been down here the whole time. 

So, no. No, no, no. Please, I am asking you as a human being to a human being, stop asking me this question. Write down 'no'. Put a circle around it. Highlight it in neon yellow. Whatever you have to do to make it stick in your brain. Just please, stop asking me.
Have you ever had a period of time when your mood was elevated, you felt extremely energetic, or you needed less sleep but still had lots of energy?

Wait. Did you... did you actually just ask a different question? Wow. Okay. I was legitimately starting to think we were going to be stuck on that other one until the sun went down. 

Okay, elevated mood. Energetic. Less sleep. No. No, Doc, I haven't. 

Honestly, I don't think I've ever felt 'extremely energetic' a single day in my life, even when I was a rookie fresh out of the academy. I mean, I'm a guy who works a beat. My energy has always come from a thermos of cheap coffee and the adrenaline of a dispatch call, not from some... some internal battery that just never runs out. I've never been the life of the party or the guy bouncing off the walls. 

Even back when my life was normal, before the duplex and the divorce, I was a solid seven-to-eight-hours-a-night guy. If I pulled a double shift and had to be in court the next morning, and I only got three or four hours of sleep? I felt it in my bones the entire next day. I was dragging. I wasn't waking up after a quick nap feeling like I could build a house or run a marathon. I needed my rest, or I was completely useless. I've never had a time where I just didn't need sleep but felt great anyway. That sounds like something out of a comic book.

And now? For the last fourteen months? Energy isn't even in my vocabulary. I sleep, or at least I lay there on the couch staring at the ceiling, feeling like my entire body is made out of lead. Just getting up to fill Buster's water bowl feels like I'm trying to walk through wet cement. I don't have any energy at all, let alone 'lots' of it. So, no. I've never had a period where my mood was elevated or I didn't need sleep. I don't even know what that would feel like.

Have you ever had a time in your life before this current period when you felt so down or lost interest in things for at least two weeks that it affected your daily life, even if it didn’t last as long as this time?

Doc... are we really circling back to this? I feel like I'm on the witness stand and you're the defense attorney just... just trying to rephrase the exact same question to see if I trip up or change my story. 'Before this current period.' I mean, I don't know how many different ways I can explain the timeline of my own life to you. 

Look, I spent over two decades working a beat. You see things. You see terrible, messy things that most people shouldn't ever have to look at. Car wrecks, domestics, kids in bad situations... you name it. And yeah, sometimes you have a rough shift. Sometimes I'd come home and just need to sit on the back porch with a cold beer and not say a word to anybody for an hour. But did it ever turn into two weeks of feeling so down that it affected my daily life? Did I ever just stop caring about my hobbies or my job? No. Absolutely not.

Well, it's... it's hard to explain exactly when it all started, but mostly I just don't feel like myself anymore. I mean, I've always been a guy who gets things done, you know? You have to be in my line of work. Being in protective services, you have to be on the ball, alert, always moving, always ready to respond. I worked hard for my bachelor's degree, worked hard to get where I am. But lately... I just feel completely hollowed out. 

I stopped doing everything that used to make me, well, me. I stopped hiking. I used to go up the trails at the state park every single weekend with my gear, just to get away and breathe the air, but I haven't been out there in months. I stopped coaching the youth league, which I used to love. I stopped playing my guitar—it's an old acoustic I've had for twenty years, and now it just sits in the corner gathering dust because I can't even bear to pick it up. I don't even call people back anymore. My friends, my coworkers, they leave voicemails and I just stare at the phone. It's not that I don't care, it's just... I don't know. 

I live in this small rental right now, and honestly, some days I just sit in there for hours. I'll sit on the edge of the couch, or just at the kitchen table, staring at nothing for hours on end. And the most frustrating part is that I know there are things to do. The whole time I'm sitting there, my brain is listing off all the chores—the laundry piling up, the mail I need to open, the fact that I need to shower or eat a real meal—so I know I need to get up. But I just can't make myself start. It's like the starter motor in my head is completely blown. I just sit there frozen, wasting the entire day, and I can't seem to break out of it no matter how hard I tell myself to just move.

I remember back in, I don't know, maybe 2010 or 2011, I had this really bad flu. I mean, it knocked me flat on my back, sweating through the sheets, couldn't even keep a glass of water down kind of flu. Unusually high? Like... extremely energetic? No, no, definitely not. I mean, I'm a pretty even-keeled guy. Or, well, I always was. In protective services, you know, you really can't be bouncing off the walls or flying off the handle. You have to maintain a baseline. If you're too hyped up, you make mistakes, you misjudge a situation, and in my job, mistakes mean people get hurt. So I've always prided myself on being steady. 

And as for being irritable... I mean, sure, I get annoyed. Who doesn't? You get a rookie on your shift who doesn't know how to properly log an incident, or you're stuck in gridlock traffic on the interstate after a 14-hour day, yeah, you get a little grumpy. I've never been the type to just snap or lose my temper in a way that scared anybody or made them think I was acting strange.

My ex used to actually complain about it, saying I was too predictable, too routine-oriented. I like my schedules. I like knowing exactly what's coming next. I've never been one to get these huge, uncontrollable surges of energy where I'm acting like a different person. I was just... steady. Always steady. Just putting one foot in front of the other, day in and day out. Until the bottom completely dropped out of everything and now I'm just... stuck.
